explanations.explanation: Saul, baker. The verse says the LORD delivered David "from the hand of all his enemies and from the hand of Saul" (2 Samuel 22:1). Everybody else gets lumped together as "all his enemies," and Saul gets his own name tag. I think David wants us to notice that.

Goliath is the big name, so I see why he jumped out at you. But he isn't named in this song at all. The verse says the LORD delivered David "from the hand of all his enemies and from the hand of Saul" (2 Samuel 22:1). Sometimes the biggest name in your head isn't the one on the page.

Absalom is another name from David's life, but this verse doesn't use it. The word "enemies" can make your brain start flipping through a whole list. David puts one name in, and it's Saul: "from the hand of all his enemies and from the hand of Saul" (2 Samuel 22:1).

Yes, friend. Every one of those is somewhere you run when trouble is chasing you. David even says it outright: "My God is my rock, in whom I take refuge" (2 Samuel 22:3). When the sky opens up, nobody sprints toward a gift shop.

Worship is a wonderful thing, but that's not what these four pictures are about. Look at how David talks: "My God is my rock, in whom I take refuge" (2 Samuel 22:3). A refuge is somewhere you go to be safe. Then he adds, "You save me from violence."

Nobody is haggling inside a fortress, baker. David calls God "My stronghold, my refuge, and my Savior," and then says, "You save me from violence" (2 Samuel 22:3). Those are words for a person who needs somewhere safe. Nobody is shopping in that verse.

Saved is the word. David says, "I will call upon the LORD, who is worthy to be praised; so shall I be saved from my enemies" (2 Samuel 22:4). Look at the order: he calls, and then he's saved. I think it's a comfort that the first step is just calling out.

Hidden fits all that fortress talk, I'll give you that. But David's word is different: "so shall I be saved from my enemies" (2 Samuel 22:4). Hide-and-seek is a game, and this verse isn't playing one. Saved is what he says.

Running is a natural guess when enemies are around. But in this verse David isn't going anywhere. He's calling on "the LORD, who is worthy to be praised," and he says, "so shall I be saved from my enemies" (2 Samuel 22:4). That word is saved.

explanations.answer: He cries out to the LORD
explanations.explanation: He cries out. David says, "In my distress I called upon the LORD; I cried out to my God" (2 Samuel 22:7). When you're tangled up, you don't need a speech. I think that's what makes this verse so easy to remember.

Fighting loose is what I'd try first, and I'd end up more tangled than a phone charger at the bottom of a bag. But that's not what David says he did. He says, "In my distress I called upon the LORD; I cried out to my God" (2 Samuel 22:7). His first move was to call out.

Calling the soldiers sounds like a reasonable plan for a king. But the verse doesn't mention any. David says, "In my distress I called upon the LORD; I cried out to my God" (2 Samuel 22:7). The one he calls is the LORD.
The song says the opposite, baker. "And from His temple He heard my voice, and my cry for help reached His ears" (2 Samuel 22:7). The cry doesn't get lost on the way. It reaches His ears.

False, and what a verse that is. David says, "And from His temple He heard my voice, and my cry for help reached His ears" (2 Samuel 22:7). His cry reached all the way to God. I'd read that one twice.

That's the reason David gives. "The earth shook and quaked; the foundations of the heavens trembled; they were shaken because He burned with anger" (2 Samuel 22:8). If it were me standing there, I'd be hanging onto the counter with my mustache. The verse tells us the reason for the shaking, and it's His anger.

An army can rattle a road, but there's no army in this verse. David says the earth and the heavens were shaken "because He burned with anger" (2 Samuel 22:8). Even the foundations of the heavens trembled. That's a lot bigger than marching feet.

The sea does show up later in the song, in verse 16, but it isn't the reason here. In verse 8 David says the earth and the heavens "were shaken because He burned with anger" (2 Samuel 22:8). The reason comes right in the same verse.

True. David sings, "He mounted a cherub and flew; He soared on the wings of the wind" (2 Samuel 22:11). A cherub is a winged heavenly being, and the picture is the LORD in motion. You can almost feel the wind in that verse.

Look again, baker, because it's right there. David sings, "He mounted a cherub and flew; He soared on the wings of the wind" (2 Samuel 22:11). It's in the song just like that. The wings are in the verse twice, the cherub's and the wind's.

The song says the opposite, friend. After the thunder, "He shot His arrows and scattered the foes; He hurled lightning and routed them" (2 Samuel 22:15). The foes don't hold their ground. They scatter and they're routed.

False. David says, "He shot His arrows and scattered the foes; He hurled lightning and routed them" (2 Samuel 22:15). Scattered and routed means nobody stood their ground. David's foes didn't have a chance.

explanations.answer: He reaches down and draws him out
explanations.explanation: That's it. David sings, "He reached down from on high and took hold of me; He drew me out of deep waters" (2 Samuel 22:17). It's like someone grabbing your hand on a slippery dock. The LORD doesn't watch from a distance. He takes hold.

explanations.answer: He calms the waves all around him
explanations.explanation: Calming the waves would be a fine rescue, but it's not the one David describes. He says, "He reached down from on high and took hold of me; He drew me out of deep waters" (2 Samuel 22:17). David is drawn out of the water. The verse doesn't say the waves were calmed.

explanations.answer: He sends an angel to lift him up
explanations.explanation: There's no angel in this verse, baker. David says, "He reached down from on high and took hold of me; He drew me out of deep waters" (2 Samuel 22:17). Look at who's doing the reaching: He is. It's up close and personal.

Right there in the verse: "He rescued me because He delighted in me" (2 Samuel 20 is not it, it's 2 Samuel 22:20). David gives one reason, and it's the LORD's delight. I think that's worth reading twice.

David does cry out in 2 Samuel 22:7, but that's not the reason he gives for the rescue. He says, "He rescued me because He delighted in me" (2 Samuel 22:20). Nothing in the verse mentions begging long enough. The reason is the LORD's delight.

Insults aren't in this verse, friend. After bringing David out into the open, the song says, "He rescued me because He delighted in me" (2 Samuel 22:20). The reason David names is the LORD's delight in him. That's the one the song gives.

explanations.answer: He kept the ways of the LORD
explanations.explanation: That's what he points to. David says, "For I have kept the ways of the LORD and have not wickedly departed from my God" (2 Samuel 22:22). It's a personal thing: the LORD's ways, and not wickedly leaving Him. The next verses keep going in the same direction.

explanations.answer: He won every battle he fought
explanations.explanation: David does talk about battles later in the song, but that's not what he points to here. He says, "For I have kept the ways of the LORD and have not wickedly departed from my God" (2 Samuel 22:22). The victories aren't his evidence. The ways of the LORD are.

explanations.answer: He built the LORD a temple
explanations.explanation: Building a temple isn't on David's list, baker. The only temple in this song is the LORD's, where "He heard my voice" (2 Samuel 22:7). What David points to is this: "For I have kept the ways of the LORD and have not wickedly departed from my God" (2 Samuel 22:22).
David says the opposite, friend. He sings, "For all His ordinances are before me; I have not disregarded His statutes" (2 Samuel 22:23). Nothing is set aside. They're right in front of him.

False. David says, "For all His ordinances are before me; I have not disregarded His statutes" (2 Samuel 22:23). It's like me keeping the recipe card propped up where I can see it every time. His ordinances are in front of him, not on the shelf.

True. David sings, "To the faithful You show Yourself faithful, to the blameless You show Yourself blameless" (2 Samuel 22:26). He says it straight to God. Faithful to the faithful, and it's right there in the song.

It's actually in the song, baker. David tells God, "To the faithful You show Yourself faithful, to the blameless You show Yourself blameless" (2 Samuel 22:26). Those are David's words, aimed straight at the LORD. So this one is true.

Close, but the verse picks a different word. David sings, "to the pure You show Yourself pure, but to the crooked You show Yourself shrewd" (2 Samuel 22:27). Crooked and shrewd are not the same word. The verse says shrewd.
False. The verse says, "to the pure You show Yourself pure, but to the crooked You show Yourself shrewd" (2 Samuel 22:27). The word is shrewd, not crooked. One little word makes all the difference.

That's what David sings. "You save an afflicted people, but Your eyes are on the haughty to bring them down" (2 Samuel 22:28). Notice the two halves: the afflicted get saved, and the haughty get brought down. Same song, two very different directions.

Strength isn't what the verse is about, friend. David says, "You save an afflicted people, but Your eyes are on the haughty to bring them down" (2 Samuel 22:28). The haughty aren't rewarded. They're the ones being brought down.

More time isn't in this verse, baker. David sings, "You save an afflicted people, but Your eyes are on the haughty to bring them down" (2 Samuel 22:28). The purpose the song gives is bringing them down. Nothing about extra time.

explanations.answer: Charge an army and scale a wall
explanations.explanation: Yes. David sings, "For in You I can charge an army; with my God I can scale a wall" (2 Samuel 22:30). I get winded climbing onto a cooling rack, so a WALL is a lot. Notice where the power comes from: "in You" and "with my God."

explanations.answer: Rule the land without any help
explanations.explanation: Without any help is the opposite of this verse, baker. David says, "For in You I can charge an army; with my God I can scale a wall" (2 Samuel 22:30). Look at the little words: "in You" and "with my God." He's not doing it alone.

Egypt and chariots aren't in this verse, friend. David says, "For in You I can charge an army; with my God I can scale a wall" (2 Samuel 22:30). Charging and climbing are the two things he names. And both are done "in You."

That's the answer, baker. David asks, "For who is God besides the LORD? And who is the Rock except our God?" (2 Samuel 22:32). It's the kind of question where the whole room goes quiet. Nobody raises a hand.

That's not what David is asking for. He says, "For who is God besides the LORD? And who is the Rock except our God?" (2 Samuel 22:32). He isn't asking anyone to make a list. The questions are there to say there's no other God besides the LORD.

No priests in this verse, friend. David asks, "For who is God besides the LORD? And who is the Rock except our God?" (2 Samuel 22:32). He isn't handing the question to anyone. He's already answered it by asking it.
Battle. David sings, "He trains my hands for battle; my arms can bend a bow of bronze" (2 Samuel 22:35). Notice who does the training: He does. David isn't saying he taught himself.

Hands that build are good hands, but that's not David's word. He sings, "He trains my hands for battle; my arms can bend a bow of bronze" (2 Samuel 22:35). The word is battle, and the bronze bow backs it up.

Shepherd's hands are good hands, and David did tend sheep (1 Samuel 16:11). But in this song he says, "He trains my hands for battle; my arms can bend a bow of bronze" (2 Samuel 22:35). The word here is battle.
True. David sings, "my arms can bend a bow of bronze" (2 Samuel 22:35). I once tried to bend a paper clip and the paper clip won. Bronze is a whole different level.
It's right there in the song, friend. David says, "my arms can bend a bow of bronze" (2 Samuel 22:35). He says it right after, "He trains my hands for battle." So this one is true.

Yes! David sings, "You have given me Your shield of salvation, and Your gentleness exalts me" (2 Samuel 22:36). In a song full of bows and walls and fortresses, the soft word is the one that lifts him. I think that's worth noticing.

David is giving the credit away here, baker. He sings, "You have given me Your shield of salvation, and Your gentleness exalts me" (2 Samuel 22:36). It's "Your gentleness," meaning God's. The strength talk in verse 35 also begins with "He trains my hands."

His army isn't mentioned in this verse, friend. David says, "You have given me Your shield of salvation, and Your gentleness exalts me" (2 Samuel 22:36). What lifts him is "Your gentleness." That's God's gentleness.
Almost, but the second half flips it. David sings, "You broaden the path beneath me so that my ankles do not give way" (2 Samuel 22:37). The path gets wider and his ankles hold. They do not give way.
False. David says, "You broaden the path beneath me so that my ankles do not give way" (2 Samuel 22:37). A wider path and steady ankles. I don't even have ankles and I love this verse.
Strength. David sings, "You have armed me with strength for battle" (2 Samuel 22:40). He says it to the LORD. Once again, the strength is something he was given.
Wisdom is a great gift, but it isn't the word in this verse. David sings, "You have armed me with strength for battle" (2 Samuel 22:40). The word is strength. He says it directly to the LORD.

Armor sounds like just what you'd be armed with. But David's word is different: "You have armed me with strength for battle" (2 Samuel 22:40). It's strength. The song talks about a shield earlier (2 Samuel 22:36), but here it's strength.
The verse says the opposite, baker. David sings that they looked "to the LORD, but He did not answer" (2 Samuel 22:42). It's a sober line. The song doesn't say anything more about it.
False. David sings that they looked "to the LORD, but He did not answer" (2 Samuel 22:42). It's a heavy line, and I think it's fine to let it sit. The song doesn't say anything more about it.

Strife. David tells the LORD, "You have delivered me from the strife of my people" (2 Samuel 22:44). That one is close to home, because it's trouble among his own people. The song doesn't give more details than that.
Hunger isn't in this verse, friend. David says, "You have delivered me from the strife of my people" (2 Samuel 22:44). The word is strife. He's talking about his own people.
Sickness isn't in this verse, baker. David tells the LORD, "You have delivered me from the strife of my people" (2 Samuel 22:44). The word is strife. It's about his own people.

That's what the song says. "Foreigners cower before me; when they hear me, they obey me" (2 Samuel 22:45). It's a picture of David as the head of nations. The foreigners don't come with a fight. They cower.
No mocking in this verse, friend. David sings, "Foreigners cower before me; when they hear me, they obey me" (2 Samuel 22:45). The word is cower. And they obey him.

explanations.answer: They march out to fight him
explanations.explanation: Marching out to fight isn't what the song shows. David sings, "Foreigners cower before me; when they hear me, they obey me" (2 Samuel 22:45). The next verse says they "come trembling from their strongholds" (2 Samuel 22:46). That's trembling, not swinging.

It's the other direction, baker. David praises "the God who avenges me and brings down nations beneath me" (2 Samuel 22:48). The nations are brought down, not lifted up above him. It's one little word, but it changes the whole picture.
False. David praises "the God who avenges me and brings down nations beneath me" (2 Samuel 22:48). Beneath, not above. The song is clear on that.

explanations.answer: Praise the LORD and sing to His name
explanations.explanation: That's his promise. David sings, "Therefore I will praise You, O LORD, among the nations; I will sing praises to Your name" (2 Samuel 22:50). Praise and song, out loud, among the nations. That's a man who isn't done saying thanks.

explanations.answer: Build altars to the LORD in every land
explanations.explanation: Altars aren't in this verse, friend. David sings, "Therefore I will praise You, O LORD, among the nations; I will sing praises to Your name" (2 Samuel 22:50). His promise is praise and song.

explanations.answer: Send gifts to the LORD from every land
explanations.explanation: Gifts aren't in this verse, baker. David sings, "Therefore I will praise You, O LORD, among the nations; I will sing praises to Your name" (2 Samuel 22:50). The thing he promises is praise. He'll sing among the nations.

Yes, and it's the very last line of the song. "He shows loving devotion to His anointed, to David and his descendants forever" (2 Samuel 22:51). Notice that word "forever." It reaches way past David's own lifetime.

The song reaches further than that, baker. David says God "shows loving devotion to His anointed, to David and his descendants forever" (2 Samuel 22:51). It isn't David alone. His descendants are in there, and so is "forever."

explanations.answer: The soldiers who fought beside him
explanations.explanation: The soldiers aren't named in the closing verse, friend. David says God "shows loving devotion to His anointed, to David and his descendants forever" (2 Samuel 22:51). The ones named are David and his descendants.

True. The song ends, "He shows loving devotion to His anointed, to David and his descendants forever" (2 Samuel 22:51). Samuel anointed David back in 1 Samuel 16:13. Now the song comes back around to it.
It's right there in the last line, baker. "He shows loving devotion to His anointed, to David and his descendants forever" (2 Samuel 22:51). "His anointed" is David. So this one is true.
